catalog_quote: [Hoijer 1943, p.38] In the Apachean sub-stock are found six mutually unintelligible idioms: Navaho, San Carlos, Chiricahua-Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan, and Kiowa-Apache. The following remarks on pitch accent apply with equal force to each of these languages ... An utterance in the Apachean languages, phonetically considered, is a succession of evenly stressed syllables each of which possesses a clearly defined pitch accent or tone. Though speakers of these languages, like those of any other, vary the accentual patterns of their utterances in response to emotional and other non-linguistic factors, these variations are individual and haphazard. In other words, there are no distinctive accentual patterns characteristic of the word, the phrase, or the sentence which stand over and above the accentual [p.39] patterns formed by the succession of syllables constituting the utterance. The only tonemes with which we have to deal, then, are those which belong to the syllable. [p.41] a toneme count made in connected Chiricahua Apache text. Here, out of a total of 5388 syllables, 5211, or more than 96%, have a level tone. || [Hoijer 1946, sec.2:1 p.56, snippet-grade] The Chiricahua Apache utterance, phonetically considered, is a succession of evenly stressed syllables separated from one another by "valleys" or minima of prominence. [p.57] 4. Each syllable possesses a toneme. ... 5) The pitch accent of a word is built up of the tonemes of its constituent syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word stress: syllables of an utterance are evenly stressed; prominence contrasts are carried by syllable tone (high, low, falling, rising), the word's pitch pattern being just the sum of its syllable tonemes; no accentual pattern belongs to the word as such.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described (no stress contrasts at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Hoijer 1943 notes only 'individual and haphazard' emphatic/emotional variation; Hoijer 1946 notes slight intensity minima between syllables as syllable-boundary cues, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the utterance/word as phonetically observed in connected speech and citation forms; Hoijer 1946 is specifically Chiricahua (speakers at Mescalero, NM, fieldwork 1930s); Hoijer 1943 explicitly extends it to Chiricahua-Mescalero as one idiom. Note the 1946 passage was read via search-inside snippets of a borrow-only scan, with page numbers fixed from running headers in the snippets; the 1943 text is complete held by the project.
new_statements.identity_note: Hoijer 1946 describes Chiricahua Apache specifically (speakers then resident on the Mescalero Reservation, NM); Hoijer 1943 and 1938 treat Chiricahua and Mescalero as mutually intelligible varieties of one language ('Chiricahua-Mescalero'), matching Glottolog mesc1238 / ISO apm. No separate statement for the Mescalero variety beyond the 1938 note that both 'employ pitch accent as a syllable phoneme'.

sources.citation: Hoijer, Harry. 1939. Chiricahua loan-words from Spanish. Language 15(2): 110-115.
sources.note: p.111 rule 1: 'Spanish accented vowels are replaced by Chiricahua vowels with either a high or a falling tone. Unaccented Spanish vowels assume the low tone in Chiricahua.' Spanish stress is borrowed as tone; indirect support that Chiricahua has no stress phoneme. No direct stress statement.

sources.citation: Hoijer, Harry (ethnological notes by Morris E. Opler). 1938. Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache Texts. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
sources.note: Key to the phonetic system: 'Both Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache employ pitch accent as a syllable phoneme.. Two pitch registers are distinguished together with two inflected tones.. Falling and rising tones occur only in syllables with long vowels.' The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the volume (a full-text search for stress/accent full scanned) -- silent on stress.
